item.title: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live
item.snippet: Congressional districts and historic places, for mapping the rights and responsibilities in your own community.
item.description:
Question: Where do we use our rights and carry out our responsibilities?

Ideas for one lesson in MapMaker (choose any):

  • Zoom to your community and sketch pins on public places such as the courthouse, a polling place, city hall, the library, a newspaper office and a place of worship, and label each with a right in the Bill of Rights or a citizen's responsibility. Choosing public places rather than homes keeps students' addresses private.
  • Switch on the National Register layer to find historic public buildings nearby.
  • Click inside your congressional district to see who represents it now.
  • Download an image or export a PDF of the map to keep the work.

Notes: The midterm elections are on 3 November 2026. California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah have new congressional districts for the 2026 elections (National Conference of State Legislatures, September 2026), so in those states the district on the ballot can differ from the 119th Congress districts shown here.

Sources: U.S. 119th Congressional Districts and National Register of Historic Places, from the MapMaker catalogue.

Version 1.2 (14 October 2026).

item.title: U.S. 119th Congressional Districts
item.snippet: Congressional districts are regions of nearly equal population within a state. Each district is represented by one person in the House of Representatives. This layer shows the 119th (January 3, 2025 – January 3, 2027) Congressional Districts. It was built with data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives.
item.description:
The United States of America has three branches of government: the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch. The Executive Branch is led by the President and is responsible for enforcing the laws of the country. The Judicial Branch works to interpret and review the laws of the country and ensure they align with the Constitution.  This is the Supreme Court and the federal district courts. 

Finally, the Legislative Branch makes the laws. It is composed of two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives. The Senate has 100 members, two from each of the 50 U.S. States. Each Senator serves a six-year term. The House of Representatives is made up of 435 members. Each Representative serves a two-year term. Each state has a different number of seats in the House of Representatives based on its population. For example, California has 52 representatives as it has the highest population. Whereas, Alaska, Delaware, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, and Wyoming only have one representative each due to their lower populations. For much of history, representative seats were added to the House after every census as the country’s population grew. However, the number was capped in 1941 to 435 members.

Each representative represents a congressional district. A congressional district, also called an electoral district, is a geographic area of nearly equal population that elects a representative to the House. Each state draws its own districts every ten years after the decennial census. This is a process called redistricting. How these districts are drawn often impacts which political party (Democrat or Republican) has the most representatives in Congress.

Sometimes, the states draw congressional districts to represent one political party more favorably than the other. This is called gerrymandering. This makes elections less competitive and can mean one person’s vote matters more than another person’s in a different place. If this is the case, citizens of the state can take the matter to court. If the court agrees that the congressional district maps are unfair to voters, the state must redraw the maps to be fairer. Researchers at Princeton University maintain a Redistricting Report Card. How is your state doing?

Congressional districts are sometimes used for other purposes as well. For example, they are sometimes used to better understand the demographics of a particular place but the Census Bureau. They sort the information they collect into congressional districts, so they know more about the social, economic, and housing situation of each district. This can help representatives make policy decisions about the place they represent.

This layer illustrates the 119th (January 3, 2025 – January 3, 2027) Congressional Districts. The map maker used data on the location of the districts from the U.S. Census Bureau and joined it with data on each elected official from the Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives. The layer uses the congressional districts drawn from the 2020 Census. You can use the legend to see what party represents each congressional district or click on a district to see the name of the representative. Who is your representative?

item.title: United States National Register of Historic Places
item.snippet: The National Park Service’s National Register of Historic Places contains more than 90,000 historical buildings, sites, structures, and objects judged worthy of preservation. Explore those in or near your community with this map layer.
item.description:
The National Park Service’s National Register of Historic Places is a list of historical buildings, sites, structures, and objects judged worthy of preservation. It was established in 1966 when Congress passed the National Historic Preservation Act. Since then, more than 90,000 places have been added to the list due to their archeological, architectural, artistic, cultural, engineering, or historical significance.

According to the National Park Service, for a place to be considered for the National Register of Historic Places, it must meet at least one of the following criteria:

  1. The place must be related to events that have made significant contributions to history.
  2. The place is associated with a significant historical figure.
  3. The place has distinctive characteristics (type, period, or construction method) or represent a notable craftsman or artist.
  4. The place contains or might contain artifacts from history or prehistory.

Each place on the National Register of Historic Places is sorted into one of the following categories:

  • Building—Any building created to house a human activity (for example, a place of worship, house, barn, hotel, or theater).
  • Structure—Any building created for a purpose other than housing a human activity (for example, bridge, aircraft, bandstand, canal, lighthouse, or tunnel).
  • Object—Small constructions that are primarily artistic (for example, fountains, monuments, sculptures, or statuary).
  • Site—A location with archaeological (prehistoric or historic), historic, or cultural significance (for example, battlefield, ceremonial site, petroglyph, or shipwreck).
  • District—An area with a significant group of buildings, structures, objects, or sites united by a historic event or unique architecture (for example, business district, canal system, estates and farms, or rural villages).

Anyone can nominate a place to be added to the National Register of Historic Places. One starts at their state, the federal, or tribal historic preservation office where they can download the required forms to begin the process. The nominated place is then reviewed by the state historic preservation office and the state’s National Register Review Board. These two entities will notify affected property owners and if they object, or in the case of a district, if a significant portion of the property owners object the process stops. If the office and board agree that the property should be added to the register, they will submit it to the National Park Service to make the final decision.

This vector dataset in this map layer is from the National Park Service. Each location on the National Register of Historic Places is marked with a point. Each category is represented by a unique color. Due to the large number of places on the list, the map maker chose to make each point visible only at regional and local scales.

Look at the map. Is there a location on the National Register of Historic Places near you? Have you visited this place? Is there a place in your community that you think needs to be protected? Does it qualify to be added to the National Register of Historic Places?
